column2:
Each authority of the U.S. government, defined by what it does (power to take final and binding action), not its size or label.

  • Excludes Congress, federal courts, territories, D.C., courts-martial and military commissions, military authority in the field.
  • A one-person office can be an agency.
  • The President is not an agency (constitutional avoidance).

column1: What is an organic statute, and why is it your first stop?
column2: The act that creates, empowers, defines, and limits an agency. The agency's power is whatever it grants, and it also sets the procedural quadrant (formal/informal, rule/order). Born by Congress, must die by Congress: the President can hollow out an agency but not abolish it.

column1: Formalism vs. functionalism in separation of powers
column2:
• Formalism: follow the text and the specific constitutional recipe; each branch exercises only its own kind of power. Ex: Chadha majority, Buckley, Scalia in Morrison.
  • Functionalism: ask whether the arrangement threatens the core functions or balance of the branches; tolerate blending. Ex: White in Chadha, Morrison majority, Breyer in Free Enterprise Fund.

column1: The nondelegation doctrine: Rehnquist's three-part statement (Benzene)
column2:
A delegation is permissible only if:

  1. Congress made the important choice of social policy;
  2. Congress supplied an intelligible principle to guide discretion; and
  3. The principle is judicially reviewable against ascertainable standards.

Short: Congress makes the big call and gives a standard a court can measure the agency against.

column1: Is the nondelegation doctrine dead or alive?
column2:
• Dead: Whitman v. American Trucking; the intelligible-principle bar is so low nothing fails.
  • Coming back: changed Court; Gundy is the closest it has come to revival.
  • Larsen's take: it never died. Avoidance (Benzene), the removal cases, and the MQD are built around the delegation anxiety.

column1: Remedy for an impermissible delegation, and the Benzene alternative
column2: Strike down the statute. Or (the Benzene move) read the broad provision (§ 6(b)(5)) together with a narrowing one (§ 3(8)) to avoid the constitutional problem. This is how the NDD operates today: by narrowing statutes, not striking them.

column1: Industrial Union Dep't v. American Petroleum Inst. ("Benzene")
column2: Held: OSHA must first make a threshold finding of significant risk before setting the most stringent feasible standard. Read alone, § 6(b)(5) would be an unconstitutional "sweeping delegation," so read it with § 3(8). Classic constitutional avoidance. ($284M to protect 35,000 workers; 10 ppm → 1 ppm.)

Held: Delegation to the Sentencing Commission to write binding guidelines is constitutional. 3 goals, 4 purposes, 7 factors = sufficiently specific; an expert body suits a labor-intensive task.

Scalia, dissenting: a "naked" grant of lawmaking power, not ancillary to executive or judicial power; the intelligible-principle test is "flabby."

Held: SORNA's delegation to the AG about pre-Act offenders is fine. First construe the statute: it required applying SORNA to all pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, so the delegation was narrow. Closest the Court has come to reviving the NDD.

Codes of "fair competition" written by trade/industry representatives, no review process, no guidance on what "fair competition" means. Unconstitutional delegation, including to private actors. The only rule cannot be "make rules."
Delegation of legislative power to a private actor (coal industry standards). First time the Court said no to this. Not even an intelligible principle can save it.
The "death certificate" of the NDD. Scalia: "a certain degree of discretion, and thus of lawmaking, is inherent in most executive or judicial action." Delegation upheld.

column1: Private delegation: the two key questions (Ass'n of American Railroads)
column2:
1. Is the entity really private? Profit motive / fiduciary duty to shareholders, funding and ownership, who appoints the board, FOIA, Congress's label (relevant but not controlling, Lebron).
  2. Is it wielding legislative power or something short of it? Advice, guidance, an industry vote, even a veto = OK. Making or co-authoring rules = not OK.

No intelligible principle saves a private delegation.

column1: Ass'n of American Railroads v. DOT (D.C. Cir.)
column2: Held: Amtrak (treated as private) could not co-develop binding performance standards jointly with the FRA, with an arbitrator able to side with Amtrak. Two concerns: private delegation saps democratic accountability, and private entities pursue private gain, not the public good. (Later reversed: Amtrak is governmental; arbitration clause severed.)
Congress's label of an entity as "private" is relevant but not controlling. Whether an entity is governmental for constitutional purposes is for the Court.

column1: How may Congress control a delegation?
column2:
• OK: statutory overrides (amend the statute, overrule specific actions), appropriations, legislative history, the CRA (satisfies bicameralism and presentment).
  • Not OK: a legislative veto of agency action that is legislation (Chadha).

Principle: private companies can veto but not co-author; Congress can override but not veto.

Held: The one-House legislative veto is unconstitutional. Action that has the purpose and effect of altering legal rights, duties, and relations of persons outside the legislative branch is legislation and needs bicameralism and presentment.

White, dissenting (functionalist): Congress routinely delegates; it should be able to reserve a check.

Within 60 legislative days, Congress may pass a joint resolution of disapproval (majority vote, President signs). The rule never takes effect, and the agency may not reissue a "substantially similar" rule without new authorization. Rules only, not adjudications. OIRA decides what is a "major rule" ($100M+ annual effect). Bites mostly when one party holds both Houses and the White House.

1. Is the person an officer? If not, an employee, and no appointment problem.
  2. Inferior or principal? Principal = President with Senate advice and consent.
  3. If inferior, appointed by the President alone, a Court of Law, or a Head of Department, and does a statute so provide?

column1: Who is an "Officer of the United States"?
column2:
Significant authority pursuant to the laws of the United States (Buckley) + a continuing position established by law (Germaine; Lucia).

  • Significant authority = a portion of sovereign power, power to bind third parties or the government.
  • Continuing = not transient or incidental; need not be permanent.

column1: Inferior vs. principal officer: the Morrison factors and Edmond
column2:
Morrison: (a) removable by a higher executive officer? (b) only certain limited duties? (c) limited jurisdiction? (d) limited tenure?

Edmond: inferior if she has a superior other than the President, i.e., her work is directed and supervised by a Senate-confirmed officer.

Arthrex: at-will removal is not enough; needs substantive review of decisions.

Held: FEC commissioners appointed by the Speaker and President pro tem violate the Appointments Clause. Enforcement power + power to seek judicial relief = significant authority, so they are officers. Congress may not appoint its own officers to exercise executive power. Source of the officer test; the Appointments Clause is a specific recipe N&P can't override.

Held: The independent counsel is an inferior officer (removable by AG for good cause, limited duties, limited jurisdiction, limited tenure), so a court may appoint her; a for-cause limit is fine if it doesn't impede the President's take-care duty.

Scalia, dissenting: never defines "inferior"; she's harder to remove than a principal officer; a power grab.

The Tax Court's Chief Judge may appoint special trial judges.

  • Majority: the Tax Court is a "Court of Law" (not limited to Art. III).
  • Scalia (concurring): the Chief Judge is a "Head of Department"; a department is a self-contained unit, not just a cabinet post.

Both are good law; Free Enterprise Fund later adopted Scalia's definition of "department."

column1: What is a "Head of Department" for appointments?
column2: Head of a "freestanding component of the Executive Branch, not subordinate to or contained within any other such component" (Free Enterprise Fund, adopting Scalia in Freytag). So the SEC, a multi-member body, is a Department and the Commission is its Head.

column1: May Congress give an existing officer new duties without a new appointment? (Weiss)
column2: Yes, if the new duties are germane to the old office and Congress isn't aggrandizing itself (creating an office and picking who fills it). Weiss: commissioned military officers could become military judges without reappointment.
Recess appointments: the vacancy may predate the recess; a recess of fewer than 10 days is presumptively too short; the Senate is not in recess during pro forma sessions.

Held: SEC ALJs are officers (continuing career position + significant authority like Freytag STJs; their decisions can become final without Commission action). Appointment by SEC staff was invalid; a Head of Department must appoint.

Breyer: decide on statutory grounds, to avoid a Free Enterprise Fund removal problem.

Held: Administrative patent judges can't issue final, unreviewable decisions as inferior officers. Fix: sever so the PTO Director can review PTAB decisions. "Diffusion of power carries with it a diffusion of accountability." Inferior status needs substantive supervision of decisions, not just removability.

column1: The four textual options for removal
column2:
1. Impeachment only.
  2. Removal is executive; the President's power is unlimited (Vesting Clause). Myers; now Slaughter.
  3. Removal follows the mode of appointment (Senate concurrence).
  4. Congress sets the terms (N&P Clause). Humphrey's.

President Wilson could remove a postmaster without Senate consent. Vesting + Take Care = unlimited removal power over purely executive officers. Taft: the President can't execute the laws without his people in office. Backed by the Decision of 1789.

FDR could not remove an FTC commissioner protected by "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance." The FTC was quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial, so Myers didn't control. Opened the door to independent agencies. OVERRULED by Trump v. Slaughter (2026) except for bodies exercising no executive power.
Congress gave itself a role in removing an officer (Comptroller General) who executes the law. Unconstitutional. The paradigm congressional power grab.

Held: Two layers of for-cause removal (PCAOB removable only for cause by SEC Commissioners who are themselves for-cause) violate Article II; the President can't hold anyone accountable for the Board. Breyer, dissenting: functional approach; the Board needs independence.

Held: For-cause protection for a single-director independent agency (CFPB) is unconstitutional. Single head + budget independence = too much unchecked power; a novel structure. Remedy: sever the removal restriction; Director removable at will.

Held: The FTC's for-cause removal provision is unconstitutional; Humphrey's overruled except for entities exercising no executive power ("If anything more is left of Humphrey's, we overrule it"). Executive power includes rulemaking, enforcement, and in-house adjudication that is part of an enforcement scheme. Accountability, single executive, liquidation by practice.

1. Entities exercising no executive power.
  2. The Federal Reserve (distinct tradition of the First and Second Banks).
  3. Non–Article III courts (Tax Court, Court of Federal Claims), bodies that only adjudicate.
  4. Inferior officers (Morrison, Perkins).

Held: Federal Reserve Governors keep for-cause protection. The President must show a cause that implies unfitness for office, not a wish for a "more congenial replacement," with notice and an opportunity to respond. Independence and the appearance of independence matter for monetary policy.

column1: Running a removal problem on the exam (post-Slaughter)
column2:
1. Identify the agency, who is protected from whom, the officer's role, inferior or principal.
  2. Is it the Humphrey's setup? Now unconstitutional; check the carve-outs.
  3. Does the officer exercise executive power? (The whole ballgame.)
  4. Call out the weird stuff: Congress in removal (Bowsher), double for-cause (FEF), single director and budget independence (Seila), novelty.
  5. Remedy: sever the removal restriction.

All executive power is vested in one person, so the President must control all discretionary executive decisions. Strict version: (1) unlimited removal (Myers); (2) complete control over executive policymaking; (3) Congress can't give executive duties to anyone outside presidential control. Justification: accountability. Everything turns on identifying "executive power." Support: Zivotofsky v. Kerry.
The President has the exclusive power to recognize foreign governments; Congress can't force State to list "Israel" as birthplace for Jerusalem-born citizens. Cited for the unitary executive.
With Morrison, authority for congressional limits on the removal of inferior officers.

column1: Article III: the master rule and exceptions
column2:
Only Art. III judges (life tenure, salary protection) exercise the judicial power, except:

  1. Territorial courts;
  2. Courts-martial (Dynes v. Hoover);
  3. Claims against the United States;
  4. Public rights assigned to agencies, if they pass Schor/Stern balancing (and Jarkesy if a jury right is in play).

column1: Schor/Stern balancing: can a non–Article III body decide it?
column2:
1. How broad is the agency's adjudicative jurisdiction?
  2. How much Art. III supervision (standard of review, finality)?
  3. Public right or private right? (emphasized after Stern)
  4. What concerns drove Congress to depart from Art. III?
  5. Did the parties consent to this forum?

Held: The CFTC may decide a state-law counterclaim in a reparations proceeding where the parties consented (Schor chose the forum). Narrow jurisdiction, Art. III courts retain power, no real SOP threat. Brennan, dissenting: only three exceptions (territories, courts-martial, public rights); convenience isn't enough.

Held: A bankruptcy court lacked constitutional authority to enter final judgment on a state-law tortious interference counterclaim ($400M, Anna Nicole Smith estate). A private, common-law claim is outside the public-rights exception. Public right = integrally related to a particular federal government action.

• Northern Pipeline: matters between the government and individuals arising from the political branches' constitutional functions, historically decidable by them alone; not state-law claims.
  • Stern: integrally related to a particular federal government action; derives from a federal regulatory scheme.
  • Jarkesy: matters historically determinable exclusively by the political branches. Customs, immigration, tariffs, public benefits/patents, OSHA compliance, Indian tribes, public lands.

column1: SEC v. Jarkesy: the Seventh Amendment jury test
column2:
Jury required where:

  1. The claim is legal in nature: look at the remedy (money that punishes or deters = legal; restoring the status quo = equitable) and whether the cause of action has a common-law analogue; and
  2. The public-rights exception doesn't apply.

Short: common-law ancestor + punitive money remedy = jury.

Held: A securities-fraud defendant facing civil penalties has a jury right; the SEC can't adjudicate in-house. Securities fraud mirrors common-law fraud; penalties are legal. Granfinanciera controls; Atlas Roofing distinguished (compliance claim, not common-law). Dissent: breaks precedent, Atlas Roofing above all.

No jury needed where the government sues in its sovereign capacity to enforce public rights created by statute (OSHA workplace-safety penalties). Distinguished, not overruled, by Jarkesy: a regulatory-compliance claim, not a common-law one.

Fraudulent-conveyance claims in bankruptcy need a jury: traditional legal claims go to courts "whether they originate in a newly fashioned regulatory scheme or possess a long line of common-law forebears." The controlling analogy in Jarkesy.

• Schor: a private right pulled into an Art. I forum. Balancing test. May a non–Art. III body decide this at all?
  • Jarkesy: does the Seventh Amendment require a jury, so the agency can't keep it in house?

Both run through the public-rights exception, which is why they get confused.
First recognized the public rights exception: the government could collect an overdue balance from a customs collector without a jury or an Art. III court.
Approved the general permissibility of agency adjudication, in dicta.
The Seventh Amendment reaches a statutory claim if it is "legal in nature." Cited in Jarkesy for the remedy-focused inquiry.

• Informal rulemaking: § 553 notice and comment.
  • Formal rulemaking: §§ 556–557 (triggered via § 553(c)).
  • Informal adjudication: § 555 (really § 555(e)).
  • Formal adjudication: §§ 554, 556–557.

Congress picks the quadrant in the organic statute. Ask: (1) rule or order? (2) formal or informal?

An agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy, including rate-setting (rates, wages, prices, corporate structures).
A final disposition in a matter other than rulemaking, including licensing. In effect, anything that isn't a rule. Licensing is always an order even though it operates prospectively.

Generalized, forward-looking action affecting many people alike → no hearing required (Bi-Metallic: 40% increase on all Denver property). Specific, backward-looking action substantially affecting a small group → notice and hearing required (Londoner: paving assessment on one street's owners).

column1: Londoner v. City and County of Denver (1908)
column2: Held: Due process required notice and a hearing before a special assessment on the specific owners whose street was paved. Where the power to tax is delegated, taxpayers need a stage at which to be heard.

column1: Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization (1915)
column2: Held: No hearing required for a general 40% increase in valuation of all Denver property. Where many are affected the same way, they are "heard" through the political process.

column1: Which definition of "rule" do you use?
column2:
• Constitution / due process, or a non-APA statute → common-law Bi-Metallic/Londoner (forward-looking + general = rule).
  • Choosing an APA quadrant → § 551(4).

Significant regulatory actions go to OIRA (in OMB, the White House) for cost-benefit review before taking effect. OIRA can approve, return, or extend review past 90 days. A White House check on rulemaking.

column1: § 559: the APA doesn't displace other law
column2: The APA does not repeal or limit additional procedural requirements imposed by statute or otherwise recognized by law. Challengers' best textual argument in Vermont Yankee.

column1: The six sources of procedural obligations
column2:
1. The APA (the default, not the exclusive source);
  2. Other statutes, especially the organic statute;
  3. The Constitution (Due Process);
  4. The agency's own regulations (agencies can bind themselves);
  5. Past agency practice;
  6. Judicial gloss on all of the above.
Statute requires action "on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing." "After hearing" alone is not enough (Florida East Coast).

column1: United States v. Florida East Coast Ry. (1973)
column2: Held: ICC Act's "after hearing" did not trigger formal rulemaking; written submissions sufficed. Across-the-board per diem rates were a legislative-type judgment, not adjudication of specific facts. Practically ended formal rulemaking.

column1: § 554(d): separation of functions in formal adjudication
column2: The presiding employee may not consult anyone on a fact in issue ex parte, and may not be supervised by agency employees engaged in investigative or prosecuting functions.

column1: § 557(b): agency review of an initial decision
column2: The ALJ's initial decision becomes the agency's decision without further proceedings unless appealed or reviewed. On review, the agency has all the powers it would have had in making the initial decision (it can redo the facts).

The proponent bears the burden of proof; sanctions must rest on reliable, probative, and substantial evidence; parties may present oral or documentary evidence and cross-examine as may be required for a full and true disclosure. In rulemaking or initial licensing, the agency may use written submissions where a party won't be prejudiced.

column1: Is a statutory "hearing" formal or informal? The three options
column2:
1. Presume informal unless Congress clearly wanted formal (City of West Chicago, 7th Cir.).
  2. Presume formal for adjudication subject to judicial review (Seacoast, 1st Cir.).
  3. Defer to the agency's reasonable reading (Chemical Waste, D.C. Cir.). Majority view; survives Loper Bright via statutory stare decisis.

Argue all three on the exam.

column1: City of West Chicago v. NRC (7th Cir. 1983)
column2: A license amendment under AEA § 189(a) "hearing" did not require a formal hearing; presume informal absent clear contrary intent, and defer to the NRC's reading of its regulations. Option One.

"After opportunity for public hearing" on a specific discharge permit → formal adjudication; a quasi-judicial decision subject to review must be on the record (the Administrator couldn't rely on a study outside the record). Option Two.
Whether "hearing" means a formal hearing is a question the agency may answer; defer to its reasonable reading (Chevron). Option Three, now the majority view.

column1: The three steps of § 553 notice and comment
column2:
1. Notice in the Federal Register of the proposed rule's terms, substance, or the issues involved.
  2. Comment: written data, views, or arguments, oral optional. No hearing, no cross-examination.
  3. Concise general statement of basis and purpose.

Plus § 553(d): generally publish 30 days before the effective date.

column1: Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. NRDC (1978)
column2: Held: Courts may not impose rulemaking procedures beyond the APA (e.g., cross-examination), absent constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances. The APA is the maximum courts may require.

column1: Hybrid rulemaking requirements that survive Vermont Yankee
column2:
1. Adequate notice: disclose the data that animated the agency's thinking.
  2. Logical outgrowth: the final rule can't differ so much that the proposal didn't give notice.
  3. Respond to significant comments: those that, if true, would require a change.

They survive because they beef up Steps 1 and 3, not Step 2.

column1: Substantive vs. procedural vs. interpretive rules vs. policy statements
column2:
• Substantive (legislative): creates rights/obligations; force of law; needs N&C.
  • Procedural: governs the agency's own procedures; no N&C.
  • Interpretive: clarifies rather than creates; no force of law; no N&C.
  • Policy statement / guidance: announces factors or tentative goals (often enforcement); no N&C.

column1: Guidance/interpretive rule vs. legislative rule: the three tests
column2:
1. Practical impact on the agency: does the agency intend to bind itself? (U.S. Telephone Ass'n v. FCC)
  2. Fairly encompassed: does it refine rather than change the regulation? (Air Transport Ass'n v. FAA)
  3. Binding norms: prospective only, and genuinely leaves the agency and the public free? (PPCC v. Shalala)

Run all three.
The FCC's forfeiture schedule was a legislative rule needing N&C: applied in 300 cases with only 8 deviations, none from the schedule. The practical-impact test.

column1: Air Transport Ass'n of America v. FAA (D.C. Cir.)
column2: The FAA's Whitlow letter (crew rest measured by actual flight time) was an interpretive rule, exempt from N&C: it was fairly encompassed in the regulation and refined rather than changed it.

column1: Professionals & Patients for Customized Care v. Shalala (5th Cir. 1995)
column2: The FDA's pharmacy-compounding guide (9 non-exhaustive factors) was a general statement of policy: prospective and left the agency free to exercise discretion. The binding-norms test.
Skip N&C if the agency finds and explains that it would be impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. Narrowly construed; burden on the agency. Invoked for about 40% of rules.

column1: Factors courts weigh on good cause
column2:
1. Harm from delay.
  2. Burden is on the agency.
  3. Agency foot-dragging undercuts the claim.
  4. The value of the N&C being skipped.

Emergencies and tight statutory deadlines count.

Good cause existed for the AG's interim SORNA rule without an emergency: real harm from delay (offenders evading registration). The AG's 7-month drafting didn't defeat it. Concurrence: harmless error.
No good cause where FERC could point to only one instance of harm. Good cause is "narrowly construed and only reluctantly countenanced"; burden on the agency.
HHS health-worker COVID vaccine rule upheld without N&C on good cause. The agency must point to something specific; its own delay undercuts an emergency claim.

column1: § 555(e): the only APA rule for informal adjudication
column2: Prompt notice of the denial of a request, with a brief statement of the grounds. That's all the APA requires, but § 706 review still applies.

column1: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe (1971)
column2: Review of informal adjudication (I-40 through a Memphis park) must be on the whole administrative record, not post hoc litigation affidavits. Arbitrary-and-capricious review is a "substantial inquiry." § 701(a)(2) is very narrow: only where there is "no law to apply."
Review is presumed. Exceptions: (1) a statute precludes review; (2) action committed to agency discretion by law (no law to apply; read narrowly).

Held: An agency's decision not to enforce (FDA and lethal-injection drugs) is presumptively unreviewable under § 701(a)(2). Rebuttable where the statute gives enforcement guidelines (Dunlop v. Bachowski: "shall investigate… shall bring"). Rescinding a rule or denying a rulemaking petition is different.
A court may uphold agency action only on the grounds the agency itself relied on. If those grounds are inadequate, remand; the court can't substitute a better rationale.

The choice between rulemaking and adjudication is in the agency's informed discretion; it may announce new standards in an adjudication even with retroactive effect. Jackson, dissenting: "administrative authoritarianism."

column1: DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of California (2020)
column2: Chenery I applied to the DACA rescission: the agency's new, post hoc justifications couldn't be considered.

• Adjudication: retroactivity generally OK, unless it replaces a reasonably clear old policy that induced reliance (then prospective only); clarifications OK absent manifest injustice.
  • Rulemaking: presumption against retroactivity; Congress must authorize it with a clear statement.

column1: APA recap: the "fast & flimsy" three steps
column2:
1. Rule, order, or "off the grid" (an exemption)?
  2. Did Congress want it formal or informal?
  3. Were the quadrant's required procedures followed? If not, invalid. Procedural challenges are reviewed de novo. Check other sources of procedure too.

column1: Procedural due process: the two questions
column2:
1. Is there a protected interest (life, liberty, property)?
  2. If so, what process is due? (Mathews v. Eldridge)

Property requires a legitimate claim of entitlement, more than an abstract need or unilateral expectation, from an independent source: statute, contract, regulation, rules, or mutually explicit understandings (Roth; Perry). The old right/privilege distinction is gone.

1. The private interest affected;
  2. The risk of erroneous deprivation under current procedures and the value of additional safeguards;
  3. The government's interest, including fiscal and administrative burdens.

Judged by the generality of cases.

Held: No evidentiary hearing required before terminating Social Security disability benefits. Less dire private interest than welfare (not need-based); medical evidence is documented and reliable; government burden is high.

Held: Welfare recipients get a pre-termination evidentiary hearing: oral presentation, cross-examination, decision on the record, statement of reasons. Recipients depend on aid to live. "The opportunity to be heard must be tailored to the capacities and circumstances of those who are to be heard."
Held: An untenured professor on a one-year contract had no property interest in renewal and no liberty interest (free to work elsewhere, no stigma). Established entitlement theory.
Held: A nontenured professor may have a property interest from "mutually explicit understandings": a de facto tenure program in the faculty handbook.
Damage to reputation alone isn't a protected liberty or property interest. Needs "reputation-plus": some other tangible loss (a job, a license).
Plurality: no liberty interest in living in the U.S. with a noncitizen spouse.

The county couldn't keep the $25,000 surplus from selling a home for a $15,000 tax debt. Decided under the Takings Clause (notes file it under property). Pair with Webb's Fabulous Pharmacies (interest on funds held by government isn't public money).

column1: APA § 706(2): grounds for setting aside agency action
column2:
(A) arbitrary, capricious, abuse of discretion, or not in accordance with law;

(B) contrary to the Constitution;

(C) in excess of statutory authority;

(D) without procedure required by law;

(E) unsupported by substantial evidence (formal / on-the-record cases);

(F) unwarranted by the facts (trial de novo cases).

Review the whole record; rule of prejudicial error. § 706(1): compel action unlawfully withheld.

column1: The four categories of question an agency answers
column2:
1. Fact: answered without reference to a legal standard.
  2. Law: meaning of a statute, regulation, or constitutional provision.
  3. Mixed: applying a legal standard to particular facts.
  4. Policy: legislative-like judgment or discretion.

Exam rule: always identify which one the agency answered.

column1: Common-law spectrum of standards of review (most to least aggressive)
column2: No deference → de novo → clearly erroneous → abuse of discretion → reasonable jury → total deference. (Anderson v. Bessemer City: clearly erroneous for trial-court facts; law de novo.)
Supplies a default cause of action for review of agency action. Review is presumed, and it is hard to challenge agency action outside this cause of action.

Substantial evidence is judged on the record as a whole, including the examiner's (ALJ's) findings the Board rejected. Less deferential than the jury standard, more than clearly erroneous; ALJ credibility findings carry weight.
Scalia equated substantial evidence with a reasonable-jury standard, in tension with Universal Camera. Larsen treats substantial evidence as still more aggressive than the jury standard.
A vocational expert's refusal to produce underlying job data doesn't categorically defeat substantial evidence; the threshold is not high and deference goes to the ALJ.
Courts defer on fact-bound, law-application questions (a coal-tax independent-contractor arrangement); abstract legal questions are de novo.

What "employee" means in the abstract = question of law, de novo. Whether newsboys are employees = mixed question; accept the Board's view if it has "warrant in the record" and a "reasonable basis in law."

Agency interpretations get weight according to their "power to persuade": thoroughness, validity of reasoning, consistency, and all other factors (contemporaneity, expertise). On-call firefighter overtime. Still good law, and revived after Loper Bright.

Two steps: (1) Has Congress directly spoken? (2) If not, defer to a reasonable agency interpretation. Upheld EPA's plantwide "bubble." OVERRULED by Loper Bright (2024); prior holdings keep statutory stare decisis.

Held: § 706 requires courts to use independent judgment on questions of law; no deference just because a statute is ambiguous. Chevron overruled. Ambiguity isn't delegation; courts are the experts on law. Kagan, dissenting: Congress prefers agencies fill gaps; 40 years of acquiescence; stare decisis.

1. Using independent judgment, what is the best reading of the statutory phrase?
  2. Has Congress delegated authority to the agency to decide (e.g., "define," "appropriate," "reasonable," fill up the details)? If so, police the limits of that delegation.
  3. Does the agency's view deserve Skidmore respect?

1. How clearly must Congress delegate discretion ("expressly delegate," "fill up the details," "appropriate/reasonable")?
  2. Do mixed questions still get deference (Hearst)?
  3. Will agencies dress up legal interpretation as policy?
  4. What will the Skidmore revival look like (contemporaneous, consistent)?

column1: Why would a judge defer to an agency?
column2:
• Defer: expertise a judge lacks (technical, industry, the organic statute); cheaper and efficient; finality and clarity; respecting the delegation.
  • Never defer: agencies may be biased or captured; worsens NDD anxieties; value of an independent judiciary; agencies aren't experts on everything; respect the APA compromise (judicial "homework checking").

On questions of vast economic and political significance, the agency needs clear congressional authorization. Statutory, not constitutional, but motivated by nondelegation and separation-of-powers concerns.

Politically controversial or salient; lots of money; expansion of executive power into a new lane; core constitutional powers (taxing); new readings of old statutes; big changes that short-circuit legislation; an "unheralded" claim of power.

column1: MQD: linguistic canon or substantive canon?
column2:
• Barrett: a linguistic canon, how a reasonable speaker understands a delegation in context (the babysitter example). Fits textualism.
  • Gorsuch: a substantive canon that protects separation of powers and nondelegation values, like constitutional avoidance.

FDA lacked authority to regulate tobacco: Congress wouldn't hand off a decision of such economic and political significance cryptically, and it had legislated relying on FDA's disclaimer of authority. An MQD forerunner.
"Exchange established by the State" includes federal exchanges, but the Court decided it itself, no Chevron, given the question's significance and that it's outside the IRS's expertise.
The CDC's nationwide eviction moratorium exceeded the Public Health Service Act. Major question.
OSHA's vaccine-or-test mandate for employers with 100+ employees exceeded its authority. Major question.
EPA's generation-shifting Clean Power Plan needed clear congressional authorization, which was lacking. Solidified the MQD by name.
The HEROES Act's "waive or modify" allows modest adjustments, not mass student-loan cancellation. Barrett concurrence: MQD as a linguistic canon (the babysitter).

Held: IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. "Regulate … importation" can't bear that weight; the taxing power is Congress's; no MQD exception for the President. Gorsuch (substantive canon), Barrett (linguistic), Kagan et al. (ordinary interpretation) concurring; Kavanaugh, Thomas, Alito dissenting (foreign-affairs exception).
Courts defer to an agency's interpretation of its own ambiguous regulation unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation. Kept but cabined by Kisor.

column1: Kisor v. Wilkie: when does Auer deference apply?
column2:
1. The regulation is genuinely ambiguous after exhausting all traditional tools;
  2. The agency's reading is reasonable;
  3. The character and context warrant controlling weight: the agency's official position, implicating its substantive expertise, reflecting fair and considered judgment (not a litigating position, post hoc rationalization, or unfair surprise).

Otherwise, Skidmore weight only.

Vietnam veteran's PTSD benefits; VA's reading of "relevant" records. Held: Auer survives on stare decisis but within the limits above; remanded. Doesn't violate § 706 or § 553 (interpretive rules lack force of law, Perez). Gorsuch would overrule Auer.

Pharma detailers are "outside salesmen" exempt from FLSA overtime. No Auer deference to DOL's amicus-brief reading: unfair surprise, with massive retroactive liability, a longstanding industry practice, and no prior enforcement.

column1: Which standard applies at each layer? (Christopher chart)
column2:
• Statute: Loper Bright / Skidmore.
  • Regulation's reading of the statute: Loper Bright / Skidmore, respecting any express delegation (e.g., "define and delimit").
  • Agency's reading of its own regulation: Auer / Kisor.
